*The original encoder–decoder architecture from D2L. The diagram separates
the source encoder, the transferred state and the target decoder; it does
not specify a recurrent cell or require equal source and target lengths.
Source: Aston Zhang, Zachary C. Lipton, Mu Li, Alexander J. Smola,
[D2L, §10.6](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/encoder-decoder.html),
CC BY-SA 4.0. Complete original SVG, without cropping or redrawing.*

## Условная языковая модель

### Bridging different state shapes D2L separates decoding from the operation that prepares its initial state: > In the following decoder interface, > we add an additional `init_state` method > to convert the encoder output (`enc_all_outputs`) > into the encoded state. *Zhang, Lipton, Li, Smola, [D2L, §10.6, Decoder](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/encoder-decoder.html#decoder), original English excerpt, CC BY-SA 4.0.* Consider a two-layer bidirectional GRU encoder with hidden width 3 and a one-layer unidirectional GRU decoder with hidden width 4. Copying the encoder’s `[4,B,3]` final state into the decoder cannot satisfy its `[1,B,4]` state contract. One possible bridge takes the final forward and reverse states of the top encoder layer, concatenates them, and applies a learned affine map followed by tanh. This is a design choice, not an operation that the GRU API performs automatically. | Operation | Shape | |---|---| | Encoder final states | `[4,B,3]` | | Expose layer and direction axes | `[2,2,B,3]` | | Select the top layer | `[2,B,3]` | | Concatenate its directions for each input | `[B,6]` | | Apply the learned bridge and tanh | `[B,4]` | | Add the decoder’s layer axis | `[1,B,4]` | The six features for each input must come from that same input. For example, directly reshaping `[2,B,3]` into `[B,6]` when $B>1$ would mix the batch and direction axes. Concatenating the two direction slices avoids that error. For a concatenated vector $(0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,0,0.4)$, a bridge row $(1,0,0,1,0,0)$ and bias 0.05 give $0.1-0.1+0.05=0.05$, then $\tanh(0.05)\approx0.049958$. Each of the decoder’s four initial-state coordinates has its own learned row. The affine map has $4\cdot6+4=28$ parameters. The following standalone program isolates this interface. It processes two source sequences of different lengths, constructs a correctly shaped initial decoder state, then checks that a loss on two decoder steps reaches both the bridge and the encoder. As in the D2L-style model below, the fixed source context also accompanies every target input. The target inputs here are assigned feature vectors; the next complete model adds token embeddings, vocabulary logits and the translation loss. ```python import torch from torch import nn from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_padded_sequence torch.manual_seed(61) dtype = torch.float64 B, encoder_layers, encoder_width, decoder_width = 2, 2, 3, 4 source_features = torch.randn(B, 3, 2, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) source_lengths = torch.tensor([2, 3]) encoder = nn.GRU(2, encoder_width, num_layers=encoder_layers, bidirectional=True, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype) packed = pack_padded_sequence(source_features, source_lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False) _, encoded = encoder(packed) assert encoded.shape == (4, B, 3) by_layer = encoded.reshape(encoder_layers, 2, B, encoder_width) top = by_layer[-1] fixed_context = torch.cat([top[0], top[1]], dim=-1) torch.testing.assert_close(fixed_context, torch.cat([encoded[-2], encoded[-1]], -1)) state_bridge = nn.Linear(6, decoder_width, dtype=dtype) initial_decoder = state_bridge(fixed_context).tanh()[None] assert initial_decoder.shape == (1, B, 4) assert sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in state_bridge.parameters()) == 28 decoder = nn.GRU(2 + 6, decoder_width, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype) target_features = torch.randn(B, 2, 2, dtype=dtype) decoder_inputs = torch.cat([ target_features, fixed_context[:, None].expand(-1, 2, -1), ], dim=-1) decoded, final_decoder = decoder(decoder_inputs, initial_decoder) assert decoded.shape == (B, 2, 4) and final_decoder.shape == (1, B, 4) decoded.square().mean().backward() assert state_bridge.weight.grad.abs().sum() > 0 assert source_features.grad[0, :2].abs().sum() > 0 assert source_features.grad[0, 2].count_nonzero() == 0 assert encoder.weight_hh_l1_reverse.grad.abs().sum() > 0 example_context = torch.tensor([.1, .2, .3, -.1, 0., .4], dtype=dtype) example_row = torch.tensor([1., 0., 0., 1., 0., 0.], dtype=dtype) torch.testing.assert_close((example_row @ example_context + .05).tanh(), torch.tensor(.05, dtype=dtype).tanh()) ``` Only the top-layer states enter this bridge directly. Lower encoder layers still influence them through the recurrent network. A different model could project all layer states or initialize several decoder layers; it must define that mapping explicitly. For an LSTM decoder, both $h_0$ and $c_0$ need compatible shapes, so mapping only the hidden state is insufficient. This bridge still transfers a fixed number of source coordinates. Changing its dimensions does not give the decoder access to individual source positions. The direction/state axis ordering is specified in [PyTorch 2.14, GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html) and worked through in the [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/04 RNN, LSTM и Seq2Seq/02 LSTM и GRU#recurrent-bidirectional|previous chapter]]. ### Сдвиг целей и teacher forcing

### Reordering states after beam selection The global top-$B$ selection may keep two children of the same parent and none from another parent. Suppose the live prefixes are A and C. If the selected continuations are CB and CD, both inherit the state after C: | Selected prefix | Parent row | State to carry | Token to consume next | |---|---:|---|---| | CB | 1 | state after C | B | | CD | 1 | state after C | D | The parent state already includes the old prefix. The selected new token is then consumed by each child to obtain its state and predict the following token. Both children initially receive equal state values, but the different B and D embeddings generally make the next states different. The code below checks this one state-routing operation after selection. It does not choose the beam or compute sequence probabilities; the complete finite-distribution search above handles that separate step. ```python import torch from torch import nn torch.manual_seed(67) dtype = torch.float64 embedding = nn.Embedding(4, 3, dtype=dtype) # A=0, B=1, C=2, D=3 decoder_cell = nn.GRUCell(3 + 2, 4, dtype=dtype) parent_states = torch.tensor([ [.1, .2, .3, .4], # state after A [.5, .6, .7, .8], # state after C ], dtype=dtype) selected_parents = torch.tensor([1, 1]) selected_tokens = torch.tensor([1, 3]) # CB and CD source_context = torch.tensor([[-.2, .4]], dtype=dtype) with torch.no_grad(): inherited = parent_states.index_select(0, selected_parents) child_inputs = torch.cat([ embedding(selected_tokens), source_context.expand(2, -1), ], dim=-1) child_states = decoder_cell(child_inputs, inherited) for child in range(2): single = decoder_cell(child_inputs[child:child+1], parent_states[1:2]) torch.testing.assert_close(child_states[child:child+1], single) assert not torch.allclose(child_states[0], child_states[1]) wrong_states = decoder_cell(child_inputs, parent_states) assert not torch.allclose(child_states[0], wrong_states[0]) ``` For `nn.GRUCell`, beam rows occupy axis 0 of `[beam,m]`. For a sequence module’s hidden state `[layers,beam,m]`, the corresponding gather is on axis 1. An LSTM must reorder both hidden and cell states with the same parent indices. When decoding several source inputs together, the indices and source contexts must also remain grouped by their source. An EOS child is placed among finished hypotheses according to the chosen search rule; it is not fed back merely to continue that finished prefix. The D2L [beam-search tree](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/beam-search.html#fig-beam-search) illustrates global prefix selection. The tensor example here makes the associated recurrent-state routing explicit. ### Длина ответа и качество перевода
